name: GM2 Gangliosidosis, AB Variant (GM2 Activator Deficiency)

clinicalPearls: The rarest of the three GM2 gangliosidoses, caused by deficiency of the GM2 activator protein encoded by GM2A, rather than deficiency of the hexosaminidase enzyme itself.

Clinically and pathologically indistinguishable from classic infantile Tay-Sachs disease: normal early development followed by loss of milestones, marked startle response to sound, and progressive neurodegeneration.
A cherry-red macular spot is a characteristic ophthalmological finding, reflecting ganglioside accumulation in retinal ganglion cells with sparing of the central foveola.

Crucially, hexosaminidase A and B enzyme activities measured against standard artificial substrates are normal or near-normal, which distinguishes it from Tay-Sachs (variant B) and Sandhoff (variant O).
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating impaired hydrolysis of the natural GM2 ganglioside substrate despite normal enzyme assays, together with GM2A molecular testing.
Autosomal recessive inheritance; carrier detection and prenatal diagnosis require molecular analysis of GM2A because conventional enzyme-based carrier screening will not detect it.
Macrocephaly, hypotonia evolving to spasticity, refractory seizures, blindness and a progressive vegetative state develop in the classic infantile phenotype.
No disease-modifying therapy exists; management is supportive with attention to seizures, feeding, secretions and family support.
reference.pathophysiology: The GM2 activator protein is a small lysosomal glycolipid-transfer protein that is an obligatory cofactor for the degradation of GM2 ganglioside. It extracts a single GM2 molecule from the lysosomal membrane and presents it in a soluble complex to beta-hexosaminidase A, enabling the enzyme to cleave the terminal N-acetylgalactosamine residue. In the AB variant, biallelic pathogenic variants in GM2A abolish or cripple this activator, so even though structurally intact and catalytically competent hexosaminidase A and B are present, the natural substrate cannot be presented for hydrolysis. GM2 ganglioside therefore accumulates progressively within the lysosomes of neurons throughout the central and peripheral nervous system, causing neuronal distension with membranous cytoplasmic bodies, dendritic and axonal disruption, neuroinflammation and ultimately neuronal death. Because the biochemical block lies at the substrate-presentation step rather than at the enzyme, standard fluorogenic or chromogenic substrates, which do not require the activator, are hydrolysed normally, producing the deceptive picture of normal enzyme activity with severe in-vivo storage.
additionalDifferentials: Tay-Sachs disease (variant B, hexosaminidase A deficiency due to HEXA variants)
Sandhoff disease (variant O, combined hexosaminidase A and B deficiency due to HEXB variants)
Infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN1) presenting with regression and visual failure
Niemann-Pick disease type A with hepatosplenomegaly and cherry-red spot
Krabbe disease and other early infantile leukodystrophies
Non-accidental injury or hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy where regression and exaggerated startle are misattributed
additionalInvestigations: Beta-hexosaminidase A and B activity assay against synthetic substrates (characteristically normal, the key discriminator)
Loading or in-vitro assay demonstrating defective degradation of radiolabelled or fluorescent natural GM2 ganglioside
Molecular genetic testing of the GM2A gene to confirm biallelic pathogenic variants
Dilated fundoscopy for a cherry-red macular spot
Neuroimaging with MRI showing white-matter signal change, thalamic involvement and progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy
Electroencephalography and visual/auditory evoked potentials for seizure activity and sensory pathway degeneration
Cultured skin fibroblast studies for combined enzyme and activator function when the biochemical picture is ambiguous
redFlags: Progressive loss of previously acquired developmental milestones in an infant
Exaggerated, non-habituating startle response to sound with hyperacusis
Cherry-red macular spot with declining vision progressing to blindness
Emergent refractory seizures or myoclonus in a regressing infant
Progressive macrocephaly with feeding difficulty and recurrent aspiration
reference.prognosis: The classic infantile AB variant follows a relentlessly progressive course with neurological devastation and death typically in early childhood. Rare later-onset phenotypes progress more slowly but remain neurodegenerative.
pitfalls: Excluding a GM2 gangliosidosis on the basis of normal hexosaminidase A and B activity, thereby missing the activator-deficient AB variant.
Relying on enzyme-based carrier screening or prenatal testing, which cannot detect GM2A heterozygotes; molecular testing is required.
Attributing the exaggerated startle and regression to a non-organic or acquired cause and delaying metabolic work-up.
Confusing the cherry-red spot with other storage disorders without pursuing the specific biochemical and genetic distinction.
Assuming enzyme-replacement or substrate-reduction strategies developed for other conditions are applicable when no proven disease-modifying therapy exists.
references: Standard inborn errors of metabolism reference texts
Clinical biochemical genetics guidelines on lysosomal storage disorders
management: Provide palliative, supportive care as no curative or disease-modifying treatment is available
Control seizures with antiseizure medication and manage the exaggerated startle response
Support nutrition and protect the airway with modified feeds and gastrostomy as dysphagia progresses
Provide respiratory care, secretion management and treatment of recurrent aspiration and infection
Coordinate multidisciplinary paediatric neurology, therapy and palliative care with family support
Offer genetic counselling with molecular carrier detection and prenatal diagnosis for autosomal recessive GM2A disease, as enzyme-based carrier screening will miss it
